questions.q: What are the two main systems that coordinate responses in humans?
What is the basic functional unit (nerve cell) of the nervous system specialized to transmit electrical impulses?
Which type of neurone transmits electrical impulses from receptors (sense organs) to the central nervous system (CNS)?
What is the role of relay (intermediate) neurones?
a: To connect muscles directly to bones
To carry signals from the brain to sweat glands
To detect light in the retina
To transmit electrical impulses from sensory neurones to motor neurones within the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord)

questions.q: What is a synapse?
a: A junction where two neurones meet, across which impulses are transmitted by chemical neurotransmitters
A receptor cell in the skin

questions.q: How do nerve impulses pass across a synaptic cleft between two neurones?
a: By neurotransmitter molecules diffusing across the gap and binding to receptor proteins on the next neurone
By active transport of sodium ions
By physical contact of cell membranes

questions.q: What is a reflex action?
a: A slow, thought-out response requiring conscious brain decision-making
A rapid, involuntary, automatic response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought, protecting the body from harm

questions.q: Which of the following correctly lists the pathway of a reflex arc in order?
a: Effector -> Motor neurone -> Relay neurone -> Sensory neurone -> Receptor
Sensory neurone -> Receptor -> Spinal cord -> Effector
Receptor -> Sensory neurone -> Relay neurone (in CNS) -> Motor neurone -> Effector

questions.q: What is a hormone defined as in human physiology?
a: A chemical substance produced by an endocrine gland, carried by the blood, which alters the activity of one or more specific target organs
An electrical signal travelling along an axon
An enzyme that digests food in the gut
A white blood cell that destroys pathogens

questions.q: Where are hormones released directly into the body?
a: Into ducts leading to the skin
Into the bloodstream (blood plasma) for transport

questions.q: How does hormonal coordination compare to nervous coordination?
a: Hormonal responses are much faster and shorter-lived
Nervous responses are slower and last for days
Hormonal responses are generally slower, travel via the blood, and have longer-lasting effects compared to rapid electrical nerve impulses
There is no difference between them

questions.q: Which endocrine gland is known as the 'master gland', secreting hormones that control other glands as well as growth hormone?
What is the role of adrenaline during 'fight or flight' situations?
a: To prepare the body for action by increasing heart rate, boosting blood glucose levels, dilating pupils, and redirecting blood to muscles
To slow down breathing and promote sleep
To stimulate digestion and nutrient storage

questions.q: What hormone is produced by the thyroid gland to control the body's metabolic rate?
What is the primary difference in action between insulin and glucagon?
a: Insulin lowers blood glucose by converting it to glycogen, whereas glucagon raises blood glucose by breaking down glycogen into glucose
Insulin is a nerve signal; glucagon is a hormone

questions.q: What is negative phototropism in plants (or equivalent tropic responses)?
a: Growth away from a stimulus such as light (e.g., roots growing away from light)

questions.q: What plant hormone controls plant growth by promoting cell elongation in shoots?
How does auxin cause a plant shoot to bend toward a unidirectional light source (phototropism)?
a: Auxin is destroyed on the lit side, making that side grow faster
Auxin redistributes to the darker side of the shoot, stimulating cells on that side to elongate faster than those on the lit side, causing the shoot to bend toward the light
Auxin stops all cell division in the plant

questions.q: What is gravitropism (geotropism) in plant roots?
a: A response in which plant roots grow toward the direction of gravity (positive gravitropism)
The flowering of plants in spring

questions.q: Which of the following describes the pupillary reflex (iris reflex) in bright light?
a: Circular muscles relax, radial muscles contract, making the pupil wider
Both sets of muscles relax completely
Circular muscles contract and radial muscles relax, causing the pupil to constrict (narrow) to protect the retina from intense light

questions.q: What happens to the iris muscles and pupil size when moving from a brightly lit room into a dark room?
a: Radial muscles contract and circular muscles relax, causing the pupil to dilate (widening) to let in more light

questions.q: What is accommodation in the human eye?
a: The adjustment of the lens shape by ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments to focus on near or distant objects
The movement of the eyeball in its socket
The contraction of the iris in bright light

questions.q: How does the eye focus on a near object?
a: Ciliary muscles relax, suspensory ligaments pull tight, flattening the lens
The pupil constricts to a pinhole
Ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments slacken (loosen), allowing the elastic lens to become thicker and more curved to refract light strongly

questions.q: What happens to the ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments when focusing on a distant object?
a: Ciliary muscles contract strongly and ligaments loosen
The lens becomes spherical and thick
The iris expands to cover the lens
Ciliary muscles relax, putting tension on the taut suspensory ligaments to pull the lens into a thinner, flatter shape

questions.q: Which type of receptor cell in the retina is responsible for black-and-white vision in dim light?
Which type of receptor cell in the human retina provides color vision and functions best in bright light?
What is the fovea region of the retina specialized for?
a: High-acuity, detailed color vision containing the highest density of cone cells
Focusing light rays onto the cornea

questions.q: What is a tropism in plants?
a: A random movement in response to temperature
A chemical hormone secretion in animals
A growth movement of a plant part in response to an external directional stimulus (such as light or gravity)

questions.q: What role do neurotransmitters play in nervous coordination?
a: They diffuse across synapses to chemically transmit electrical nerve impulses from one neurone to the next
They insulate nerve fibers like myelin
They generate electrical impulses in the brain

questions.q: Which part of the central nervous system coordinates complex thought, voluntary movement, and conscious sensory processing?
What is the function of the cerebellum in the human brain?
a: To control breathing and heart rate automatically
To coordinate balance, posture, and smooth voluntary muscle movements
To process visual images from the retina

questions.q: Which brain structure controls unconscious, vital autonomic functions such as breathing rate and heart rate?
What is voluntary action compared to an involuntary reflex?
a: An action resulting from conscious decision-making originating in the cerebrum involving the brain
A response that bypasses the spinal cord entirely without nervous input

questions.q: What is the function of the myelin sheath surrounding many nerve fibers (axons)?
a: To act as an electrical insulator, speeding up the transmission of nerve impulses along the neurone
To supply oxygen to the nerve cell
To connect sensory cells to muscles

questions.q: Why are reflex actions important for survival in animals?
a: They allow animals to learn complex behaviors
They are extremely fast and automatic, minimizing potential damage to the body from harmful stimuli without requiring time-consuming brain processing
They increase metabolic rate during exercise

questions.q: What organ detects changes in blood glucose concentration and secretes the hormones insulin and glucagon in response?
